paper_title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: World models (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; 2025) predict future states conditioned on action sequences without execution in the environment. Recently, robotics world models (RWMs) (Gao et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026) realize this by building on video diffusion foundation models (Wan et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024), generating photorealistic, temporally coherent videos conditioned on robot actions. This makes them promising direction for diverse usage in evaluating policies (Guo et al., 2026; Jeon et al., 2026), planning manipulation trajectories (Assran et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), or generating training data (Jang et al., 2025). However, serving these roles requires robotics world models to faithfully reflect how small action changes alter future outcomes. For example, slight changes in reaching motion can determine whether gripper grasps an object, misses it, or pushes it away (Figure 1). Yet existing models tend to produce visually plausible videos that ignore such differences (Yang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026). Since such models predict similar outcomes for actions with different real consequences, they are unreliable as policy evaluators and mislead planners into selecting the wrong actions. Addressing this requires world models to acquire action sensitivity, and by extension, learn the relationship between action variations and resulting dynamics. We therefore treat action sensitivity as distributional problem. Rather than simply reproducing recorded futures with high visual fidelity, we argue that an RWM should capture how the distribution of future observations shifts as actions vary under given observation context. To learn such distributions, we introduce action variation directly into the training data. Specifically, we collect robot-environment interactions by running policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation, in which an operator interacts freely with objects without predefined task. Following Lynch et al. (2020), we refer to such data as play data and to this policy as the play policy. 1 Preprint Figure 1: Small action perturbations lead to distinct action effects. From the same initial state, actions drawn from narrow distribution change the grippers approach only slightly, yet produce qualitatively different outcomes, where the cube is grasped, missed, or pushed away. faithful world model must reproduce how these outcomes shift as the action is perturbed, rather than only rendering plausible video for generic actions. During data collection, we inject temporally correlated noise into the action chunks produced by the play policy before rollout and log the injected perturbations. These rollouts expose how visual outcomes vary with action changes without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state or explicit outcome labels. Building on this data, we introduce AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective that teaches the world model the relationship between action changes and their visual consequences. AFFECT explicitly uses the noise injected into the training actions to supervise how generated visual outcomes should change with those action perturbations. In this way, the model is directly encouraged to respond to action variation in the same way as the real environment, rather than merely generating visually plausible futures. Since AFFECT operates on features from frozen encoders, it can be added to existing RWMs without architectural changes. We evaluate AFFECT on simulated UR5e environment and two real-robot settings following the DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and ALOHA-2 (Aldaco et al., 2024) configurations, and apply it to two distinct backbones, DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) and Cosmos3 (Agarwal et al., 2026). To test whether the world model reflects action differences, we measure how well its predicted policy success rates correlate with real ones. On this measure, AFFECT improves every one of the six backboneembodiment combinations, for instance raising the correlation of DreamDojo on DROID from 0.468 to 0.790 and that of Cosmos3 on ALOHA-2 from 0.298 to 0.694. AFFECT also improves most visual metrics, including FVD reductions of up to 23% on DROID and gains on every metric at both short and long horizons in simulation, suggesting that learning how actions shape outcomes also helps the model predict more realistic futures. Finally, this improved sensitivity translates into better model-based planning, where AFFECT raises task success rates by around 8% on both UR5e pick-and-place and ALOHA-2 long-horizon tasks.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: A world model trained only to reconstruct recorded videos can generate realistic futures that barely depend on the supplied actions. We introduce AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective that targets this failure directly. Rather than asking each generated video to match its recorded counterpart, AFFECT asks generated videos to respond to action perturbations in the same way as recorded videos. This requires interaction data in which actions are perturbed in known way (Section 3.1) and loss that measures the response to these perturbations (Section 3.2). Section 3.3 then interprets this loss statistically. 3.1 DATA GENERATION VIA PERTURBATION PLAY Play data (Lynch et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2026), in which the robot interacts freely with its environment without task instructions, covers broad range of interactions. We train play policy on human-teleoperated play trajectories and roll it out autonomously, which requires no scene resets or task-specific procedures and therefore scales to large amounts of data. To vary actions around what the policy would do, we inject temporally correlated noise into each action chunk and execute At = clip( At + Ut), where At RHD is the nominal chunk from the play policy and Ut = (ut, . . . , ut+H1) RHD is the injected noise. We refer to each chunk, together with its context ot and recorded future Ot, as window. For each window, we log the perturbation Ut, its noise-distribution parameters, and the nominal and executed commands. We log Ut before clipping so that the logged samples follow the specified noise distribution. The world model receives only ot and At as inputs, and Ut is used only in the AFFECT loss. Because this loss compares recorded and generated videos across rollouts, each window needs single recorded future, and no repeated executions from the same starting state are required. Appendix A.1 details the collection protocol. 3 Preprint Figure 2: Overview of AFFECT. Frozen encoders ϕ, ψ extract video features from both the recorded and generated futures, and perturbation features from the logged action perturbations. Pairing the centered perturbations with each set of video features gives the recorded and predicted action effects (Φ(O), Φ( ˆO)), which measure how visual change moves with the perturbation across rollouts. The AFFECT loss optimizes over the distance between the two distributions, so that generated futures respond to perturbations in the same direction and with the same strength as real ones. 3.2 MATCHING ACTION EFFECTS WITH FROZEN ENCODERS The data of Section 3.1 pair each recorded future with the perturbation that produced it. Across many windows, these pairs reveal how the scene responds to actions. If stronger pushes tend to move an object farther, for instance, then recorded windows with stronger push will on average show the object farther away. We want generated videos to show the same tendency. To measure it, we summarize the perturbation and the video by few features each and ask how the two sets of features vary together. Frozen feature encoders. We compute these features with two fixed encoders, ψ(Ut) RKψ for the perturbation and ϕ(Ot) RKϕ for the video. Each output is simple, hand-specified quantity. perturbation feature might be the signed or squared sum of the noise over the window, and video feature might be change in per-channel mean of the video latent or projection of the latent change. Appendix A.5 lists the full feature bank. We keep both encoders frozen throughout training. If ϕ were trained jointly with the world model, it could drive the loss to zero by outputting constant, and the model would learn nothing about actions. Centering the perturbation features. Before relating the two sets of features, we need the perturbation features to vary around zero, and some of them do not. The squared noise, for example, is always positive. Multiplying it with video feature would then reward matching that feature even when the perturbation has no effect on it, so the loss would end up supervising static content such as the background. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We validate AFFECT on simulated and real-robot perturbation play. We design our experiments to investigate the following questions: Does AFFECT improve the visual/action fidelity of generated futures? (Tables 1 and 2) Does more action-faithful world model help select better actions at test time? (Figure 3) Do the frozen features actually see the action effect? (Figure 4) 4.1 ROBOTICS WORLD MODELS FOR POLICY EVALUATION Embodiments and Datasets. We consider three embodiments, each collected with the perturbation play protocol of Section 3.1. In simulation, we use UR5e manipulation environment from OGBench (Park et al., 2025). On real robots, we use Franka Research 3 in the hardware configuration proposed by DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and bimanual ALOHA-2 (Aldaco et al., 2024) setup. Every episode is single unpaired rollout, since AFFECT never uses repeated executions from the same start. Further details are in Appendix A.1. 6 Preprint Implementation details. We apply AFFECT to two action-conditioned rectified-flow backbones, DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) and Cosmos3 (Agarwal et al., 2026), which represent the state-of-theart among robotics world models. Both are post-trained from released weights on the same windows for each embodiment. For all baselines and AFFECT variants, they share the same training dataset, schedule, and initializations. We fire the AFFECT term every 8 iterations and set λ so that it is 15% of the flow loss on short calibration run. Other details are in Appendices A.2A.9. Baselines. We compare against competing robot world models as baselines for AFFECT. First, iVideoGPT (Wu et al., 2024) is an autoregressive token-based model. CoCo (Shi et al., 2026), which adds counterfactual-consistency constraints to iVideoGPT, was reproduced by us as close as possible while following their paper. As noted in their paper, the ASC2 component of their paper is not suited for joint-space actions like in our settings, so we only implement the MSC2 component. Ctrl-World (Guo et al., 2026) is video-diffusion world model for policy evaluation. We also report DreamDojo and Cosmos3 trained with the flow loss alone, which isolates the effect of AFFECT. All baselines are trained on the same perturbation-play corpora, and have fixed budget, where they see the same amount of samples during training. Evaluation. Following Ctrl-World (Guo et al., 2026), we evaluate the models in closed loop, where policies generate actions, world models predict videos conditioned on those actions, and the generated observations are fed back into the policy. We report PSNR, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), and FVD (Unterthiner et al., 2018) for single prediction window (short horizon) and for autoregressive rollouts chained over multiple windows (long horizon). To measure action fidelity, we compute the Pearson correlation between real and generated rollout success rates across policy checkpoints and tasks. Each generated video receives binary success label from human evaluators, with success labels only given when the task is clearly succeeded in the output video and the target object and environment remain visible throughout the rollout. For the DROID and ALOHA-2 setup, we utilize GR00T N1.5 (NVIDIA GEAR, 2025), FLARE (Zheng et al., 2025), and DUST (Won et al., 2026) as policy models for action generation. For UR5e on the OGBench setup, we utilize GCIQL and GCIVL policies, which are both defined in OGBench (Park et al., 2025). For each embodiment, we utilize 12 episodes per 4 checkpoints across 2 tasks. Simulation results. Table 1 reports results on UR5e. AFFECT improves both backbones on every reported metric, including video quality at both horizons and the correlation between real and imagined policy success rates. For DreamDojo, Pearson correlation increases from 0.451 to 0.686, while FVD decreases from 85 to 73 at the short horizon and from 108 to 93 at the long horizon. DreamDojo + AFFECT achieves the best score on every metric among the evaluated methods. For Cosmos3, correlation increases from 0.091 to 0.334, alongside smaller FVD reductions from 470 to 463 and from 562 to 540. These results show that the gains extend beyond single-window visual quality to policy evaluation and autoregressive rollout. Real robot results. Table 2 reports results on the DROID and ALOHA-2 configurations. On DROID, AFFECT raises Pearson correlation from 0.468 to 0.790 for DreamDojo and from 0.425 to 0.583 for Cosmos3, while reducing FVD from 807 to 622 (23%) and from 910 to 744 (18%), respectively. Both backbones also improve in PSNR and LPIPS. On ALOHA-2, Cosmos3s correlation increases from 0.298 to 0.694, the highest among the evaluated methods, while its FVD decreases from 333 to 257. DreamDojos correlation improves from 0.325 to 0.490, with PSNR increasing from 24.20 to 24.91 and LPIPS decreasing from 0.06 to 0.05, although FVD rises slightly from 183 to 188. Thus, AFFECT consistently improves agreement with real policy success rates, while generally improving visual metrics. 4.2 ROBOTICS WORLD MODELS FOR PLANNING Evaluation setup. We test whether improved action fidelity helps select actions at test time using the proposal-selection scheme of DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026). At the start of each execution horizon, 5 policy checkpoints trained on the target task are each queried for candidate action trajectories. Using the current camera frame and the candidate actions as input, the world model imagines future video for each candidate, and trained success estimator scores each video. The candidate action chunk with the highest score is executed open-loop before replanning, at which we repeat the process. We compare DreamDojo and DreamDojo + AFFECT with the same policy ensemble and success estimator. An additional baseline, Uniform, selects candidate action at random rather than utilizing 7 Preprint Figure 3: Planning with action-faithful world models. Success rates (%) of plans selected with each world model on (a) UR5e and (b) ALOHA-2, where one long-horizon task consists of three consecutive subtasks. Candidate action chunks are proposed by an ensemble of five policy checkpoints. Uniform picks one at random, while DreamDojo and DreamDojo + AFFECT imagine each chunk and select the one whose imagined video scores highest under learned success estimator. world model. The score estimator uses frozen DINOv2 features with light transformer head to predict task-success probability given video input. Further details are in Appendix A.10. Tasks and Results. For the UR5e setup, we evaluate on success rate over 5 select pick-and-place tasks from OGBench, while we use long-horizon task for ALOHA-2, consisting of 3 consecutive tasks where the robot must open trash bin, and throw away two items on the table. Figure 3 shows that average UR5e success increases from 46.7% with Uniform to 60.0% with DreamDojo and 68.3% with DreamDojo + AFFECT, an additional gain of 8.3 percentage points. ALOHA-2 results also show that AFFECT provides better environment for planning over the baseline world model, with an average gain of 8.4 percentage points. With the proposal ensemble and success estimator held fixed, the improvements show the usefulness of action-effect matching for improving model-based planning. 4.3 ANALYSIS AND ABLATIONS Do the frozen features see the action effect? The frozen video features detect action effects primarily where the robot changes the scene (Figure 4). We establish this on recorded UR5e videos by measuring the consistency of perturbationfeature associations at each latent cell. We check whether products of perturbation and video features have consistent sign across episodes, then average over feature pairs. We also evaluate on baseline setup that randomly pairs perturbations with videos from other windows, breaking the link between action perturbations and outcomes. Responses are 1.62.2 times stronger than this shuffled baseline in regions traversed by the arm, cube, or shadow, which is where action-induced visual change is concentrated, but remain at chance on the static table and backdrop. This confirms that the features provide localized action-effect signal for AFFECT. Figure 4: Action-effect localization. Frozen-feature responses on UR5e relative to shuffled pairs, where brighter cells indicate stronger responses. Ablation studies. We compare six Cosmos3 configurations after 10k training iterations on perturbation play data, evaluated on video fidelity metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, FVD) to examine the role of actionoutcome correspondence, perturbation weighting, and training-data quantity  (Table 3)  . Finally, we train the flow-only baseline and Cosmos3 + AFFECT on the same 20% subset of the training data to assess the method under limited data. sections.title: 5 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Robotics world models (RWMs). Learned world models began as compact latent dynamics models used for planning or actor-critic learning in imagination (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; 2025; Hansen et al., 2024), and have since become large video generators conditioned on actions or text (Yang et al., 2024; Du et al., 2023; Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder & Fruchter, 2025; Valevski et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024). For manipulation, the dominant recipe is to posttrain general pretrained video diffusion or flow model with action conditioning (Zhu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). These models are used to generate data (Jang et al., 2025), to plan (Du et al., 2024; Bar et al., 2025), and increasingly to evaluate policies without actual real-world rollout (Li et al., 2025; Jeon et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026). Action fidelity in world models. growing body of mostly concurrent work finds that RWMs often render plausible videos that ignore their action condition. Benchmarks pair successful and failure-inducing actions from fixed scene (Yang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026) or score robot-object interaction directly (Jiang et al., 2026), and position papers argue that counterfactual fidelity rather than visual quality should be the deciding criterion (Wang et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026). Inversedynamics probes (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Yeom et al., 2026) test action recoverability from generated video, and similar ideas have been turned into training objectives that reconstruct the action or separate predictions made under different actions (Ye et al., 2025; Han & Yilmaz, 2026; Gan et al., 2026). Because these objectives can be satisfied by distinguishable robot motion alone, they do not guarantee correct robot-object interaction. Other methods supervise outcomes directly, through replayed off-expert actions in simulation (Chen et al., 2026) or through additional outcome labels and rewards (Zhou & Zhang, 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), which limits how far they scale on real robots. AFFECT needs neither paired counterfactual rollouts nor outcome labels.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective that trains robot world models to learn how action perturbations change future observations. Using perturbation play rollouts with logged perturbations and action effect encoders to extract video/perturbation features, it adds action effect supervision without outcome labels, repeated executions from the same state, or architectural changes. Across DreamDojo and Cosmos3 backbones on UR5e, DROID, and ALOHA-2 hardware, AF9 Preprint FECT improves the correlation between real and imagined policy success rates, with improvements in most visual metrics. The additional model-based planning results further suggest that these gains can translate into better action selection. AI USE STATEMENT In this work, we used generative AI tools for editing and proofreading the manuscript text, including fixing typographical errors and checking the LaTeX source against the formatting instructions, and upscaling image resolutions for showcasing task settings. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work, and every suggested edit was checked against the source and results by the authors. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI. ETHICS STATEMENT This work trains video world models for robot manipulation and uses them to evaluate robot policies. All real-robot data were collected by the authors on Franka Research 3 and bimanual ALOHA-2 in laboratory setting, using the perturbation-play protocol of Section 3.1. Human involvement was limited to teleoperated play episodes used to fine-tune the data-collection policy and to resetting objects that left the workspace (Appendix A.1). We are not aware of other ethical concerns specific to this work. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT Section 3 and Appendix specify AFFECT in full. The data-collection protocol and per-robot configurations are in Appendix A.1. The backbones, their action inputs, and warm starts are in Appendix A.2. The feature bank, estimator, scales, sampler, and training schedule are in Appendices A.5A.9. The planning setup is in Appendix A.10. Appendix states the assumptions behind the objective. Baselines and AFFECT variants share data, initialization, and schedule, differing only in the auxiliary loss (Section 4.1). ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS This paper was supported by RLWRLD Inc. Sections A.4A.9 give the objective, the feature banks, the estimator, the per-test scales, the sampler and the training schedule. A.1 DATA COLLECTION BY PERTURBATION PLAY ON REAL ROBOTS AFFECT is trained on perturbation play. policy is run closed-loop on the real robot, and every command it issues is perturbed by noise drawn from process we control and log. Neither demonstrations of the target task nor paired rollouts are needed. Play policy and rollouts. The nominal behavior comes from generalist imitation policy finetuned on small set of human play teleoperation episodes, in which an operator interacts freely with handful of tabletop objects instead of repeating one task. We use GR00T-N1.5 with the FLARE objective (NVIDIA GEAR, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025) on both robots. At each replanning point the policy observes the cameras and the proprioceptive state, emits chunk of absolute joint-position targets, and the controller executes the first steps before the policy is queried again. Episodes are rolled to fixed step budget and never gated on success. Objects are left where the previous rollout put them, and human intervenes only to return objects that leave the workspace, so coverage grows by drift, in the spirit of autonomous play collection (Yin et al., 2026). sections.content: We provide qualitative examples of open-loop long-horizon generation in simulation (Figure 5) and on the real-world FR3 (Figure 6). In each example, the world models start from the same initial observation as the ground-truth rollout and are conditioned on the same action trajectory, so the generated videos can be compared frame by frame against the outcome that the actions actually produced. Since the generation is open-loop, the models receive no ground-truth frames beyond the initial observation, and any deviation from the ground-truth rollout therefore reflects how faithfully each model follows the conditioning actions over long horizon. The results showcase that AFFECT allows for better tracking of objects and results in higher quality representation of action effects. Figure 5: Open-loop long-horizon rollouts on UR5e in simulation. (a) Ground-truth rollout obtained by executing the action trajectory in the OGBench simulator. (b, c) Videos generated by Cosmos3 and Cosmos3 + AFFECT when conditioned on the same action trajectory. Frames are ordered in time from left to right. 26 Preprint Figure 6: Open-loop long-horizon rollouts on the real-world FR3. Each panel shows one episode. (b, c) Videos generated by Cosmos3 and Cosmos3 + AFFECT when conditioned on the same action trajectory. Frames are ordered in time from left to right. (a) Ground-truth rollout recorded while the FR3 executes the action trajectory.
